Missed ASML's Run? What Holders Had To Believe
sum: If you had put money into ASML on 5 November 2025 and simply sat on it for a year, the outcome was hard to ignore. For ASML shareholders, the return over the past year was 40.5%, including dividends. That result now sits alongside headlines about AI chip demand, new export controls and fresh record quarters. If you were weighing ASML back then, what exactly were you trading off between monopoly power on one side and rising geopolitical and competitive risk on the other?
The shares cost €907 at the start of the period, and anyone looking at ASML then had two very different stories to consider.
The bullish narrative pointed to a Fair Value of €1,000, a rough estimate of what the stock might be worth if revenue grew 17.3% a year and profit margins stayed near 29.3% over five years.
The bearish view suggested Fair Value of €769, based on assumptions of 7.2% annual revenue growth and a key risk that tighter export controls and geopolitical shocks could disrupt sales and margins.

ASML went on to report Q3 2026 revenue of €11.662b and net income of €4.960b, up from €7.516b and €2.124b in Q3 2025, with net margin rising from 28.3% to 42.5%. That strength leaned toward the optimistic case that assumed high profitability, although fresh export control headlines and new Chinese lithography capacity kept the geopolitical and competitive risks in play. Overall, the evidence cut both ways.

The key assumption that got tested was pricing power in a constrained supply chain. For any other chip equipment stock, you would now track whether higher orders and tight capacity actually show up in both revenue and net margin, rather than just in commentary about AI demand.
ASML now trades at €1,250, up 40.5% over the past year. The selected Narrative sets its Fair Value below that level, arguing the share price already bakes in a lot of good news about the business.

ASML Holding stock: AI demand stretches capacity outlook to 2030
sum: ASML's third-quarter update on October 14 underscored how artificial intelligence investment is extending demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment. In its third-quarter results release, ASML said customers were increasing short- and medium-term equipment forecasts and were expressing interest in orders for 2029 and 2030.

ASML reported third-quarter net sales of 11.7 billion euros, up from 9.3 billion euros in the second quarter. Gross margin rose to 57.5% from 54.0%, while net income increased to 5.0 billion euros from 2.9 billion euros. New lithography systems sold climbed to 113 units from 86.

Chief Executive Christophe Fouquet said customer forecasts were being driven primarily by views on the size and duration of AI-related investment. ASML now expects its currently planned supply for both 2027 and 2028 to fall short of customer demand and is investigating ways to expand 2028 capacity beyond the previously communicated 30% increase.

The company expects fourth-quarter 2026 net sales of 14.2 billion to 15.2 billion euros, with a gross margin of about 57%. Its full-year outlook calls for sales of 44 billion to 45 billion euros and a gross margin of about 56%. The outlook reflects strong demand visibility, but production expansion, customer timing and supply-chain execution remain important variables for investors.

ASML also said it purchased about 4.1 billion euros of shares under its 2026-2028 buyback program during the third quarter. An interim dividend of 1.88 euros per ordinary share was scheduled to become payable on November 4, separating the company's capital-return plans from its operating outlook.

ASML's Economic Heft Is Beyond Doubt. Its Revenue Forecast Is the Open Question.
sum: Two narratives are colliding around ASML Holding this week, and only one of them will ultimately move the stock.

On one side sits a fresh estimate from ING Research, published October 26, which sizes up just how deeply the Dutch economy leans on the chip-equipment maker. On the other, a familiar pattern of sector-wide turbulence: ASML's US-listed shares were swept into a broad semiconductor selloff on Friday after Intel delivered a disappointing outlook, while investors simultaneously began questioning the returns on the industry's massive AI infrastructure spending. No new operating statement from ASML drove that move — the uncertainty came entirely from the surrounding environment.

Then the picture shifted again. ASML shares climbed 2.1% as chip stocks staged a recovery, with memory and equipment names reportedly leading the rebound following recent steep losses. That bounce, however, is a sector story, not a company story. It offers no fresh evidence that ASML's own business prospects have improved.

The ING Research estimate puts ASML's total economic footprint for 2026 at as much as 2.2% of Dutch gross value added, with the direct contribution potentially reaching 1.6%. Both figures are projections, not settled outcomes.

The gap between the direct contribution and the broader footprint matters. The study isn't only about ASML itself — it flags the Netherlands' growing dependence on the company and on its semiconductor-equipment cluster, turning a corporate success story into a question of economic concentration.

For investors, that pivotal position is an argument for ASML's relevance. It says nothing about what the shares should be worth. Macroeconomic weight and market valuation measure different things, and conflating the two mistakes economic importance for portfolio safety. Friday's session made that distinction plain.

What actually anchors the investment case is the guidance ASML issued roughly three weeks ago. Management projected fourth-quarter 2026 revenue of EUR 14.2 billion to EUR 15.2 billion — the central yardstick against which any lasting recovery must be measured. For the full year 2026, the company forecast revenue of EUR 44 billion to EUR 45 billion.

sum: A 2.3% rebound on one trading day says little about a chipmaker whose next real verdict comes from a revenue range, not a share ticker.

ASML shares climbed 2.3% even as fresh anxieties over chip costs and the financing of the AI boom weighed on the wider sector. That gain arrived a day after the stock had slipped 2.8% in a weak technology tape, a swing that neatly captures the dilemma facing investors: do the company's business prospects justify faith in a recovery, or does the risk of a broader demand slump carry more weight?

Media reports said Apple's warning about margin pressure from higher memory-chip costs dragged European semiconductor names lower, ASML among them. Oracle's planned capital raise added a second layer of concern, reviving doubts about how the AI buildout gets funded. Neither item is an ASML warning. Neither explains the rebound, either.

Friday brought a third signal, this one from the PC aisle. Reuters reported that Intel's weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter revenue guidance, combined with worries about PC demand, set off a global selloff in chip stocks, and ASML was caught in the downdraft. The risks thus have separate origins — cost burdens, demand questions, financing doubts — and none of them automatically means ASML will miss its own numbers.

What they do raise is the bar for proof. Investors now have to judge whether the anxiety stays confined to particular corners of the market or reshapes expectations for future investment across the board.

Against that nervous backdrop, ASML disclosed further purchases under its existing repurchase program. The distinction matters more than the headline: these were executed transactions under a program already in place, not the announcement of a new one. Continuing the buyback did nothing to shield the stock from the sector's gloom, which is why the purchases offer no dependable short-term price support.

The repurchases do sit alongside the company's hard numbers as a concrete capital measure. They still leave the bigger question — whether the returns on AI spending will justify the outlay — unanswered.

ASML Keeps Buying Back Stock While Its Order Book Waits for Answers
sum: ASML has confirmed a fresh batch of share repurchases under its existing buyback programme, covering transactions executed between 26 and 30 October. The disclosure is a progress report on capital already deployed — not an expansion of the framework and not a new steer on trading.
That distinction matters. A buyback shows how the company is using its cash; it says nothing new about demand for its lithography systems. Investors should keep the two questions apart.

The scale of the underlying business is clear enough. In the third quarter of 2026, ASML posted net sales of EUR 11.7 billion and a net profit of EUR 5.0 billion. Those figures form the backdrop to the repurchases, but nothing in the latest notice alters them. Its only incremental content is the steady execution of the programme.

The latest filing follows a similar announcement on 26 October, when ASML reported the purchase of 343,310 shares for the preceding reporting week. Taken together, the two notices point to a programme being worked through methodically rather than a one-off gesture.

Alongside the buybacks, ASML is returning cash directly to shareholders. A interim dividend of EUR 1.88 per ordinary share is scheduled for payment on 4 November 2026, and the company fixed the exchange rate for payment to New York shareholders on Tuesday. Both channels of capital return, however, are separate from operating demand and from how the stock is valued — they do not answer the same question as expectations for future orders.

The buyback news lands against a tougher backdrop for chip stocks. On Friday, ASML came under pressure in a broader selloff of AI-linked technology names, triggered according to media reports by Intel's weak revenue guidance and Amazon's disclosure of heavy AI-driven cash outflows. Reuters also linked the wider weakness in semiconductor shares to doubts over the scale and returns of AI spending.

That debate stretches well beyond the near-term business outlook. Demand for equipment is only part of it; just as important is whether the planned investments can be financed and whether data centres can be built out as expected.

sum: A record quarter wasn't enough to keep chip equipment stocks out of the red after Lam Research's CFO let slip a phrase that spooked the entire semiconductor sector and sent shares tumbling hard.

A supply warning inside an otherwise record quarter is pulling chip equipment stocks lower, and the company that issued it is taking the worst of the damage. Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX | LRCX Price Prediction) stock is down 9% to $236.83 in early trading, a drop that shows how heavily a limited outlook can outweigh a strong earnings report.

Chip stocks are falling broadly after the Lam Research warning, and semiconductors are taking a harder hit than the rest of large-cap tech. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) is down 4%, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 2%, a softer decline than the chip fund’s.

Meanwhile, Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) stock is down 6% to $385.41, a smaller slide than the one hitting Lam Research shares. ASML Holding (NASDAQ:ASML) stock is down 4% to $1613.97, a far lighter loss than the one in Lam Research stock.

Lam Research reported record fiscal Q1 2027 revenue and adjusted earnings per share (EPS) above analyst estimates on October 21. Sales at Lam Research reached $8.22 billion, and non-GAAP EPS of $2.20 also beat estimates. Chief executive Tim Archer stated, “With AI driving higher semiconductor demand and greater device complexity, our focus on operational execution helped Lam deliver record revenue, profit, and earnings per share in the September quarter.”

CFO Doug Bettinger stated on the conference call that Lam Research’s December-quarter revenue guidance of $8.6 billion, plus or minus $400 million, “would have been a bit higher if not for some near-term supply chain constraints,” which the company is actively managing. Bettinger declined to put a number on the lost revenue, saying only that the guide would have been “a little bit higher.” That outlook also called for non-GAAP EPS of $2.33, plus or minus $0.15, and it outweighed the record quarter for Lam Research stock.

The update, widely reported in the media, reinforced confidence in AI infrastructure spending, and ASML rode the sector wave. The catalyst came from the market backdrop rather than from any fresh announcement by the Dutch equipment maker — a distinction that matters for anyone reading the move as company-specific news.

Super Micro's guidance concerns its own top line. For ASML, it merely underpins expectations of sustained demand across the chip sector; no new order or revised corporate forecast can be inferred from it. The advance also stands in sharp contrast to the skepticism that gripped the stock as recently as mid-October, when Reuters reported a decline for ASML amid a broader market selloff, citing doubts about the lofty expectations baked into 2028 and 2029.

On the same day, BofA Securities reiterated its buy rating on ASML, pointing to revenue and margin potential as well as possible price increases as drivers. Jefferies analyst Janardan Menon takes a more guarded view: cyclically compressing valuation multiples could cap the upside. For investors, strong demand alone does not settle the question — the price the market is willing to pay for future earnings matters just as much.

The quarterly results published roughly a week ago give the bulls operational ammunition. Gross margin for the third quarter of 2026 came in at 57.5%, and the business built on ASML's installed machine base contributed EUR 3.289 billion, or 28.2% of revenue. Upgrades to existing systems propped up margins, which means earnings do not hinge solely on how many new tools leave the factory — retrofitting machines already in the field carries real weight.

Management's guidance offers a concrete yardstick for the margin case BofA is making. For the closing quarter of 2026, ASML projected service revenue of around EUR 3.7 billion and a full-year gross margin of roughly 56%. Those figures sit alongside third-quarter revenue of EUR 11.7 billion, net profit of EUR 5.0 billion, and fourth-quarter sales guidance of EUR 14.2 billion to EUR 15.2 billion, with the full-year outlook at EUR 44 billion to EUR 45 billion.

ASML vs. Applied Digital: Which Is the Better Semiconductor Equipment Stock to Own for the Next 1 Year?
sum: ASML Holding (ASML +1.70%) and Applied Materials (AMAT +1.97%) are both benefiting from the artificial intelligence (AI) chip boom but in very different ways.

ASML's extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines are used to print the most complex circuits in leading-edge chips. As chipmakers pack more computing power into smaller chips, they need more precise manufacturing equipment. This trend has been driving demand for ASML's systems.

Applied Materials is also playing a crucial role in manufacturing advanced chips. The company supplies equipment used at several stages of chip production, including creating and shaping materials, checking for defects, and packaging chips together. Demand for these tools is rising as AI chips become more complex and increasingly use technologies such as high bandwidth memory and advanced packaging.
Let's see which stock is the better choice for investors right now.

ASML's position as the only commercial supplier of EUV lithography systems is well established. The company has exceptionally strong visibility into demand for 2027. Revenue rose by nearly 21.2% year over year to 9.3 billion euros in the second quarter of 2026 (ending June 28). The company expects net sales in 2026 to fall in the range of 43 billion to 45 billion euros.

Low-NA EUV, ASML's current-generation extreme ultraviolet lithography technology, is used to print extremely small circuit patterns on advanced chips. The company expects to increase low-NA EUV capacity by roughly 30% in 2027, from around 65 systems in 2026. Yet management says it is already close to receiving all the low-NA EUV orders it needs for 2027. This suggests production capacity, rather than a lack of customer orders, could become the bigger near-term constraint.

ASML's newer High-NA EUV technology is another potential growth driver. High-NA EUV allows chipmakers to print even smaller and more precise features on advanced chips than ASML's current EUV systems. This technology is already moving into commercial production.

sum: The semiconductor industry is playing an instrumental role in the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI). The training and deployment of AI models and inference applications wouldn't have been possible without chips, which explains why semiconductor companies have witnessed terrific growth in revenue and earnings in recent years.

Moreover, chips are also needed to run AI workloads locally on edge devices such as smartphones, personal computers (PCs), vehicles, robots, and drones, among other things. So, it is easy to see why the semiconductor industry's revenue is anticipated to jump by 64% in 2026 to $1.32 trillion, according to Gartner. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: The world's largest foundry company

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +6.33%), popularly known as TSMC, is the world's largest semiconductor foundry that manufactures chips designed by fabless chipmakers. The Taiwan-based company doesn't design its own chips. Instead, it is involved in the mass production of chips for companies such as Apple, Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm, Sony, and others, who don't have their own chipmaking facilities.

TSMC's pure-play foundry business model puts it right in the middle of the global semiconductor boom. The company's revenue has increased by 30% year over year in the first five months of 2026. TSMC has managed to build a solid customer base due to its advanced process nodes, such as 5-nanometer (nm), 3nm, and 2nm, which are more powerful and energy efficient compared to mature nodes.

This explains why major AI chip designers are designing chips based on TSMC's advanced process nodes. For instance, Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin processors utilize TSMC's 3nm process node. The robust demand for these advanced nodes explains why TSMC's foundry market share increased to 73% in Q1 this year from 68% in the same period last year, according to Counterpoint Research.
